Gini coefficient

Source: vignettes/gini.Rmd
gini.Rmd

The Gini coefficient measures inequality: how unevenly a resource is spread across the organizations in a market. It is twice the area between the Lorenz curve (the cumulative share of the resource held by the smallest pp percent of organizations) and the line of perfect equality. It is 0 when every organization is the same size and approaches 1 when one organization holds everything.

Inequality is not the same thing as concentration. Two equal organizations have a Gini of 0 but an HHI of 0.5; a market of 500 organizations with a few large ones can have a high Gini and a low HHI. Seaman et al. (2014) read values below 0.5 as reasonable equality, 0.5 to 0.75 as modest inequality and above 0.75 as high inequality.

get_gini() computes it with DescTools::Gini().

library( npcompete )
library( ggplot2 )
#> Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.4.3

# NTMAJ12 labels for the NTEEV2 major groups
ntmaj12 <- c( ART = "Arts",           EDU = "Education",
              ENV = "Environment",    HEL = "Health",
              HMS = "Human services", IFA = "International",
              PSB = "Public benefit", REL = "Religion",
              MMB = "Mutual benefit", UNI = "Universities",
              HOS = "Hospitals",      UNU = "Unknown" )

A toy market 

GEO    <- rep( c( "even", "skewed" ), each = 5 )
TOTREV <- c( 20, 20, 20, 20, 20,   2, 3, 5, 10, 80 )

toy <- data.frame( GEO, SUB = "ART", YEAR = 2020, TOTREV )

g <- get_gini( toy, geography = "GEO", subsector = "SUB", year = "YEAR" )
subset( g, GEO != "ALL" & SUB != "ALL" ) |> knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
GEO SUB YEAR N TOTREV GINI
even ART 2020 5 100 0.00
skewed ART 2020 5 100 0.82

The Lorenz curves behind those numbers:

lorenz <- function( x ) {
  x <- sort( x )
  data.frame( p = c( 0, seq_along( x ) / length( x ) ),
              L = c( 0, cumsum( x ) / sum( x ) ) )
}

curves <- rbind( cbind( GEO = "even",   lorenz( TOTREV[ GEO == "even" ] ) ),
                 cbind( GEO = "skewed", lorenz( TOTREV[ GEO == "skewed" ] ) ) )

ggplot( curves, aes( p, L ) ) +
  geom_abline( colour = "grey70" ) +
  geom_line( colour = "#3266ad", linewidth = 1 ) +
  geom_point( colour = "#3266ad", size = 2 ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ GEO ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs( x = "Share of organizations, smallest first",
        y = "Share of revenue" ) +
  theme_minimal()

Computing the Gini from org-level data

npo_panel_sample holds every 501(c)(3) filer in Vermont from 2015 to 2019, one row per organization-year. Here the market is the county.

vt <- get_gini( npo_panel_sample, geography = "COUNTY_FIPS" )

# all subsectors combined, one row per county
vt19 <- subset( vt, YEAR == 2019 & SUB == "ALL" & GEO != "ALL" )
vt19[ order( vt19$GINI ), ] |> knitr::kable( digits = 3, row.names = FALSE )

Set year = NULL to pool all years.

The Gini across US metro areas

cbsa_metrics holds every metric for every US metro and micro area (CBSA) in 2019, by NTEE major group, measured on total revenue.

metros <- cbsa_metrics
metros$NTMAJ12 <- factor( ntmaj12[ metros$SUB ], levels = ntmaj12 )

# subsector markets with at least two organizations
markets <- subset( metros, SUB != "ALL" & N > 1 & !is.na( GINI ) )

Single-organization markets get GINI = 1 by convention. They are left out of everything below.

Descriptive statistics by subsector 

markets |>
  dplyr::group_by( NTMAJ12 ) |>
  dplyr::summarize(
    metros      = dplyr::n(),
    median_N    = median( N ),
    GINI_p25    = quantile( GINI, 0.25 ),
    GINI_median = median( GINI ),
    GINI_p75    = quantile( GINI, 0.75 ),
    high        = mean( GINI > 0.75 )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
NTMAJ12 metros median_N GINI_p25 GINI_median GINI_p75 high

high is the share of metros above the 0.75 “high inequality” line. Revenue inside nonprofit subsectors is very unequal almost everywhere: most markets mix a few large organizations with many small ones.

Distribution by subsector 

ggplot( markets, aes( GINI ) ) +
  geom_density( fill = "#3266ad", colour = NA, alpha = 0.8 ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ NTMAJ12, ncol = 4 ) +
  scale_x_continuous( breaks = c( 0, 0.5, 1 ), labels = c( "0", ".5", "1" ) ) +
  labs( x = "Gini coefficient (revenue)", y = NULL ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme( axis.text.y      = element_blank(),
         panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
         panel.spacing.x  = unit( 1, "lines" ) )

The Gini and metro size

All subsectors combined, one point per metro, with a loess smooth:

all_subs <- subset( metros, SUB == "ALL" & !is.na( POP ) )

ggplot( all_subs, aes( POP, GINI ) ) +
  geom_point( colour = "grey55", alpha = 0.4, size = 1.2 ) +
  geom_smooth( method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
               colour = "#3266ad", linewidth = 1 ) +
  scale_x_log10( labels = scales::label_comma() ) +
  labs( x = "Metro population (log scale)", y = "Gini, all subsectors" ) +
  theme_minimal()

Unlike HHI, which falls as metros get larger, the Gini rises with metro size. Big metros have more organizations, which lowers concentration, but they also have a longer tail of very small organizations and a few very large ones, which raises inequality.

By subsector:

ggplot( subset( markets, !is.na( POP ) ), aes( POP, GINI ) ) +
  geom_point( colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.25, size = 0.6 ) +
  geom_smooth( method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
               colour = "#3266ad", linewidth = 0.9 ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ NTMAJ12, ncol = 4 ) +
  scale_x_log10( breaks = c( 1e4, 1e6 ), labels = c( "10k", "1M" ) ) +
  labs( x = "Metro population (log scale)", y = "Gini" ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank() )

Gini versus HHI

Inequality and concentration only loosely agree. Markets in the lower right are unequal but not concentrated: many organizations, a few of them large.

ggplot( markets, aes( GINI, HHI ) ) +
  geom_point( colour = "grey45", alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8 ) +
  labs( x = "Gini", y = "HHI" ) +
  theme_minimal()

Notes

  • The Gini of a very small market is coarse: with two organizations it can only describe how far apart they are. Filter on N before comparing markets.
  • Dorfman, R. (1979). A formula for the Gini coefficient. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 61(1), 146-149.
